what: Fluor designs and builds large, complex projects: chemical plants, mines, infrastructure, defence and government facilities, and energy installations. It also owns a substantial stake in NuScale Power, which is developing small modular nuclear reactors.
customers: Energy and chemical companies, mining groups, government agencies including the US Department of Energy and the military, and infrastructure authorities, under contracts measured in years.
money: Infrastructure, mining and metals, and advanced technologies including semiconductor plants.
Chemicals, fuels, production and energy transition projects.
Government work including nuclear site management and defence support.
moat: Very few firms can execute a multi-billion-dollar process plant or manage a nuclear site, because it requires engineering depth, a track record and the bonding capacity to guarantee the work. Government nuclear and defence contracts in particular are effectively closed to newcomers. Fluor’s value is in being one of the handful that customers will trust with a project that cannot fail.
risks: The trailing twelve months show a net loss of about $1.1B and free cash flow of roughly negative $425.0M.
Fixed-price contracting is the industry’s historical destroyer: a single badly estimated project can consume several years of profit, and Fluor has lived through exactly that.
Revenue has been flat to declining, from $16.3B in 2024 to $15.5B in 2025.
A meaningful part of the market value is the stake in NuScale, whose own share price is volatile and speculative, which makes Fluor’s valuation partly a bet on something unrelated to engineering.
Eight analysts average a $59.56 target, about 30% above the current price, on a company currently losing money.
opportunities: Cash of $2.2B against $1.1B of debt is a genuinely strong net cash position, unusual for an engineering contractor.
The shares trade at about 0.37 times sales and 6.8 times EV/EBITDA.
The shift toward reimbursable rather than fixed-price contracts removes the mechanism that caused the historic losses, if management holds the line.
Government and nuclear work is steady, long-dated and largely insulated from commercial cycles.
Data centre and semiconductor plant construction is a growing source of demand for exactly this kind of engineering capability.
watch: The mix between fixed-price and reimbursable contracts in the backlog. Fluor’s history says the contract type matters more than the backlog size, and that mix is the single best predictor of whether the losses repeat.
view: Engineering and construction contractors are a sector where the business model, not the market, determines whether shareholders make money. The work is real, the customers are serious, and the backlog looks impressive. And then a single fixed-price megaproject runs over budget, the contractor eats the difference, and several years of profit disappear. Fluor has lived this story more than once, and the trailing loss of $1.1 billion is the market being reminded of it.

The reason to look at it anyway is the balance sheet and the valuation. Cash of $2.2 billion against $1.1 billion of debt is a net cash position, which is rare in this industry and is what lets a contractor survive a bad project rather than be destroyed by one. At 0.37 times sales and 6.8 times EV/EBITDA, the market is paying very little for a business that can do things almost nobody else can — managing a nuclear site, building a multi-billion-dollar process plant, delivering a semiconductor fab.

The strategic change that matters is the shift away from fixed-price work toward reimbursable contracts, where the customer rather than the contractor carries the cost overrun. If management holds that line, the mechanism that caused the historic losses is removed, and a predictable mid-single-digit margin on $15 billion of revenue is worth considerably more than the market is paying. If the line slips when a tempting large fixed-price project appears — and it always appears — then this repeats. The backlog mix is the number that reveals it, not the backlog total.

One complication worth flagging: a meaningful part of Fluor’s market value is its stake in NuScale, a small modular reactor developer whose own share price is speculative and volatile. That means buying Fluor is partly buying an unrelated bet. It is not necessarily a bad one, but it should be sized and understood separately rather than absorbed into a view about engineering contracts. Strip it out, and the remaining business is cheap, net cash, and dependent entirely on contract discipline.
bull: The shift to reimbursable contracts holds, margins normalise on $15 billion of revenue, and a net-cash contractor at 0.37 times sales re-rates — with NuScale as free optionality.
bear: Another large fixed-price project goes wrong, the cash cushion absorbs it, and the market concludes the discipline never really changed.
